guide_sections.heading: Inspecting what each closure captured
guide_sections.body:
After `a <- make_multiplier(2); b <- make_multiplier(3)` from the reference, the enclosing environments can be read directly:

```text
expression                                   result
ls(environment(a))                           "factor"
environment(a)$factor                        2
environment(b)$factor                        3
identical(environment(a), environment(b))    FALSE
```

Each call to make_multiplier created a separate environment holding its own factor, which is why a and b do not interfere. Reading these values is useful for debugging; assigning into them from outside would hide configuration in a place no caller can see.

The threshold check in the reference uses 20 for a reason:

```text
policy                    threshold used   predicate(20)
forced at construction    10               TRUE
lazy, read at first call  100              FALSE
```

20 sits between the original 10 and the rebinding to 100, so it is the one input that separates the two policies. A test value of 5 or 200 would give the same answer under both, and the missing force call would go unnoticed.

exercises.approach: Read the call in two stages: `make_multiplier(4)` returns a function with factor 4, and `(2)` calls that function.
exercises.why: The returned function computes x times its captured factor, so 2 times 4 is 8.
exercises.wrong: Rewriting it as `make_multiplier(4, 2)`. The factory takes one argument, so R stops with an unused argument error instead of returning 8.

exercises.approach: Build `a <- make_multiplier(2)` and `b <- make_multiplier(3)` as two separate calls.
exercises.why: Each call creates a fresh environment, so a holds factor 2 and b holds factor 3, and neither reads a global setting.
exercises.wrong: Using one function that reads a global `factor` variable. Setting it to 3 for b also changes a, so a(5) becomes 15.

exercises.approach: Call `force(threshold)` in make_threshold before returning the predicate.
exercises.why: The caller sets t to 10, builds the predicate and then sets t to 100. Forcing fixes 10 at construction, so 20 counts as meeting the threshold.
exercises.wrong: Leaving out force. The promise is first evaluated when predicate(20) runs, when t is already 100, so the result is FALSE.
exercises.verify: `predicate(20)` returns TRUE, which the reference checks.

exercises.approach: Trace lazy_factory: v is 2 at construction, becomes 5, and `lazy(3)` is the first call that reads factor. Fix it by forcing the argument.
exercises.why: The promise reads v only on first use, so it sees 5 and returns 15 rather than the intended 6.
exercises.wrong: Calling `lazy(3)` once before changing v. That does evaluate the promise and fix it at 2, but the result now depends on call order, which any refactor can break.
exercises.verify: The reference `lazy(3)` returns 15; the forced `fixed(3)` from Example 2 returns 6.

exercises.approach: Force the factor, then check numeric, length one and finite before building the closure.
exercises.why: `NA_real_` is numeric and has length 1, so only `is.finite()` rejects it. Checking at construction reports the problem where the configuration was set.
exercises.wrong: Deferring the check to the inner function or skipping it. `make_multiplier(NA_real_)(2)` would then return NA, and the error, if any, appears far from the bad setting.
exercises.verify: In the reference `bad` returns TRUE, and `is.finite(NA_real_)` returns FALSE.

exercises.approach: Pass configuration as arguments or capture it with force, and avoid `<<-` updates that change behavior between calls.
exercises.why: This lesson already shows a hidden dependency: `lazy(3)` returned 15 or 6 depending on code that ran between definition and use.
exercises.wrong: A closure that increments a counter with `<<-` to label runs. Rerunning a pipeline in the same session gives different labels than a fresh session, so results cannot be reproduced.
exercises.verify: Calling `fixed(3)` before and after `rate <- 5` returns 6 both times.

run_note: The starter defines only `threshold` as 10 at the top level and prints it. Run it once, then build a factory that receives the threshold as an argument instead of reading the global. Change the global to 50 after construction and run again: a correct closure keeps the value it captured, while a function that reads the global silently changes behavior.
checks_note: The assertions confirm that the factory validates a finite numeric scalar, that `make_multiplier(4)(2)` is 8, that two closures built with different factors return 10 and 15 for the same input, that the captured predicate still accepts 20, that a lazy argument is evaluated when first used so `lazy(3)` gives 15, and that invalid configuration is rejected. They pin capture-time behavior only for these inputs; they cannot detect a closure in your own code that still reads a mutable global you forgot about, or a promise that a later change to a default argument would alter.
